title: Async prefetch + eviction race: investigation notes and short-term mitigations
content:
Summary:

Brief: Intermittent OOMs and long-tail latency spikes observed in prod serving-runtime during the week of 2025-02-10. Rootly: a race between async prefetch code path and cache eviction logic that sometimes caused KV-cache entries to be double-freed and triggered memory growth + request-level backpressure that allowed continuous-batching to accumulate huge batches (memory blowups). This doc captures notes from on-call, quick mitigations, repro attempts, telemetry discovered, and proposed runbook/engineering followups.

Impact:
- Affected customers: small subset of dedicated clusters using model-x-7B-small + enabled async prefetch.
- Symptoms: sudden node-level OOMs (OOM_killer invoked) or processes exceeding RSS and being restarted by systemd, sustained 95th/99th token latency spikes, error rate up to ~3% on a small fleet slice for ~30-90m windows.
- Frequency: ~3 incidents between 2025-02-10 and 2025-02-13, each lasting 20-120 minutes and correlated with periodic high prefix locality (same prefixes repeatedly requested).

Initial on-call notes (first responders):
- 2025-02-10 03:12 UTC: paging alerts, node host met memory threshold, SREs observed oom_kill entries in dmesg for serving-runtime process.
- Collected core dumps where available, dmesg, and PMEM stats.
- Disabled async prefetch flag on affected pool as immediate mitigation (feature-flag revert).
- Restarted a subset of nodes with drained traffic to recover steady state.
- Temporary routing policy: route traffic away from pool if memory > 85% for > 5m.

Key observations from logs and traces:
- Allocation stack traces in cores point to Buffer::reserve() called by prefetch worker and also by eviction path at near-simultaneous times.
- Heap profiles (jeprof/pprof) show large retained memory in "kv_entry->value" buffers; not reclaimed despite eviction attempts.
- Lock contention observed on kv-cache global mutex during heavy prefix churn. Contention caused prefetch workers to queue and batch up, increasing their in-flight buffered tokens, which multiplied memory usage.
- Continuous-batching queue depth rose during incidents (batch sizes up to 3x expected), suggesting batching heuristics failed to enforce per-request memory limits when prefetch backlog existed.

Hypothesis (current):
1) Async prefetch enqueues fetch tasks that allocate temporary buffers while waiting for eviction/completion.
2) When heavy prefix churn occurs, eviction triggers while prefetch is still allocating or referencing the same entries (race). The eviction path frees the entry and may place it in an object pool or call destructor while prefetch still holds a pointer -> use-after-free or double-free behavior or simply leaked buffers due to lifecycle mismatch.
3) Global cache mutex causes prefetch workers to stall; queued prefetch tasks accumulate allocated temp buffers -> RSS growth.
4) Continuous batching upstream sees requests delayed; batching windows grow and batch memory multiplies -> OOM.

Repro attempt notes:
- Deterministic reproducer is hard in unit tests because it depends on timing (prefetch latency vs eviction) and workload locality. Attempted approach: spawn N client threads to hammer a small set of prefixes with varying token lengths, enable prefetch, and toggle eviction frequency (fast TTL + small cache capacity). Observed increased RSS but not immediate OOM in local env; in k8s with node memory cgroup limit we could provoke OOM after ~30m.
- Added instrumentation (env debug build) to assert refcounts on kv_entry before free and to log prefetch task lifetimes; this helped catch 2 cases locally where prefetch held stale pointers after eviction.

Telemetry gaps discovered:
- We did not have a per-entry refcount metric exposed; only aggregate evictions/sec and cache hit ratio were monitored.
- No high-cardinality metric for prefetch-in-flight memory.
- No alert wired to large continuous-batch-size beyond a per-route slow-path counter.

Short-term mitigations (applied):
- Feature-flagged off async prefetch on affected dedicated fleets (rollout completed 2025-02-11 02:15 UTC).
- Patch: add conservative prefetch allocation cap (max_prealloc_mb_per_worker = 16MB) and immediate backpressure: if worker allocation in flight > cap, new prefetch requests are dropped/queued as low-priority. Deployed as hotfix to canary 2025-02-16.
- Add eviction hysteresis: do not evict an entry if it was allocated < 250ms ago and refcount unknown; rely on TTL/weight heuristics until safe. This is a temporary safety net.
- Routing rule: route around nodes with batch_queue_length > 200 for > 30s.

Longer-term fixes (engineering proposals):
- Implement formal refcount lifecycle for kv_entry objects with safe deallocation only when all holders release. Emit metric kv_entry_refcount_leaks and integrate with SLOs.
- Replace global cache mutex with sharded fine-grained locks or lock-free eviction queue to prevent prefetch worker stalls. Prototype already exists in branch: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/768 (note: WIP).
- Make continuous-batching respect absolute memory caps per batch and preemptively fail requests if potential batch allocation would exceed per-instance memory budget.
- Add unit/integration tests that simulate eviction+prefetch races using determinism via hooks (test-only pause points).
- Harden allocator paths: switch to scoped arenas per worker to bound temporary allocations and ensure they are freed at worker task completion.

Runbook additions (draft):
- New section: "Prefetch eviction race symptoms" under serving-runtime -> incident response.
- On alert: check metrics in order: kv_cache_evictions/sec, prefetch_worker_alloc_mb, batch_queue_depth, process_rss, oom_kill_count.
- Quick mitigation steps: 1) set async_prefetch=false via feature-flag; 2) apply routing bypass for nodes >85% RSS; 3) if persistent, scale up pool to buy time (only if capacity available).
- Must collect: pmap/ps output, jemalloc/profiler snapshot, dmesg, core if possible, per-shard eviction logs, and prefetch task trace IDs.

Ownership and next actions (owners + dates):
- Aisha P. (owner): coordinate postmortem write-up and runbook PR, due 2025-03-05.
- Miguel O. (eng): implement refcounted kv_entry prototype & perf test, due 2025-04-01.
- Samir B. (eng infra): prototype sharded-kv-lock and run heavy contention perf job, due 2025-04-15.
- Lena F. (SRE): add new Grafana panels + alerts for prefetch_alloc_mb and batch_queue_size, due 2025-03-10.

Open questions / unknowns:
- Are there other code paths that keep references to kv_entry outside of prefetch? (e.g., streaming encoder, cache-warm tasks) => search and audit required.
- How much perf does prefetch provide when safe? Can we re-enable with conservative settings without high memory risk? Need A/B experiment.
- Is jemalloc arena configuration amplifying memory retention in production builds? Consider allocator tuning audit.

Notes from debug session (useful snippets):
- dmesg snippet:
  [2025-02-11T01:23:14Z] Out of memory: Kill process 23211 (serving-runtime) score 123 or sacrifice child
  [2025-02-11T01:23:14Z] Killed process 23211 (serving-runtime) total-vm:1244828kB, anon-rss:980512kB, file-rss:2048kB, shmem-rss:0kB

- jemalloc sample (peak allocation stacks):
  1) Buffer::reserve -> prefetch_worker::do_fetch -> prefetch_scheduler -> worker_thread
  2) kv_cache::evict_entry -> entry_dtor -> release_buffer

- Lightweight reproducer commands (dev notes):
  - k6 load script hitting /generate with pinned prefix list (provided in repo under tests/eviction-race/).
  - Run local server with --enable-async-prefetch --kv-cache-capacity=256MB --prefetch-ttl-ms=50 and run the provided client with 200 concurrent virtual users.

Follow-ups logged (tickets):
- JIRA-REND-1124: "Eviction-prefetch race causing memory leaks and batch blowups" (priority P1 -> P0 on escalate)
- GH-789: minimal allocation cap hotfix PR (deployed to canary)
- GH-768: sharded-kv-lock prototype (WIP)

Closing notes:
- This incident exposed a coupling between two optimizations (async prefetch and continuous batching) that individually looked safe. Combined under certain workload patterns they amplify memory usage and reveal lifecycle bugs. The immediate safety-first approach was correct: disable the risky optimization, add conservative caps, and instrument more.
- Next major milestone: have a tested, refcount-safe kv_entry lifecycle and memory-bounded prefetch worker by 2025-04-15.

Appendix (quick checklist for on-call when reoccurrence):
- [ ] Collect full jemalloc profile (MALLOC_CONF=prof_final:true) if feasible
- [ ] Snapshot /proc/<pid>/smaps and top output
- [ ] Tag affected traces with incident_id and keep them pinned for 90d
- [ ] If multiple nodes affected, rotate to cold standby pool and avoid mass restarts

-- end of notes (working doc).
